chunks: And Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Faddal, from Ibn Bukayr, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

"It is not appropriate for a free man to marry a slave woman today. That was only when God, Exalted and Mighty, said: 'And whoever among you cannot find the means.' And 'al-tawl' (the means) is the dowry, and the dowry of a free woman today is like or less than the dowry of a slave woman."

Therefore, all these narrations indicate that the marriage of a slave woman is only permissible and allowed when the means (dowry) is lacking, and when it is present, it is disliked, although it does not invalidate the contract, because the last narration indicates this from his saying 'It is not appropriate for a free man to marry a slave woman today,' and this is a clear statement of dislike that is not a word of prohibition. And the meaning of the other narrations indicates this, as we mentioned before. The Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) said: 'If a person intends to marry another's slave woman, he proposes to her master and gives her the dowry, whether little or much. This is indicated by His Exalted and Mighty saying:

key_terms.الطَّوْلُ: The means/financial capacity (specifically referring to dowry in this context)
key_terms.الْكَرَاهِيَة: Dislikability (a legal status between permissible and forbidden)
key_terms.بِإِذْنِ أَهْلِهِنَّ: With the permission of their masters/guardians

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a free man marrying a slave woman in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi contextualizes this ruling by noting that the original Quranic permission for marrying slave women was predicated on financial inability to marry free women; however, since contemporary dowries for slave women are comparable to those for free women, the marriage is now considered disliked (makruh) rather than obligatory. The text further elucidates that such unions require the master's consent and the payment of the dowry (ujrah), establishing a clear jurisprudential framework for property rights in marital contracts within Shia fiqh.
